Ada County at a glance

Boise is both the capital of Idaho and the seat of Ada County. Population in 2025 was 546,141, and median household income in 2024 was $91,502. Inside county lines you will find Boise, Eagle, Garden City, Kuna, Meridian and Star, along with the census-designated places of Hidden Springs and Avimor.

Homes here fall into one of four school districts: Boise, Kuna Joint, Melba Joint or West Ada (Meridian Joint School District 2). Everyone also sits in the College of Western Idaho taxing zone. Your city plus your district determine which levies land on the bill, so read the levy lines on your own notice rather than borrowing a neighbor's numbers. A house in Kuna and one in Eagle can carry very different totals even when the two are worth the same on paper, simply because different taxing districts apply.

How the Assessor values a house

Every year the Assessor assigns a market value to each taxable parcel. Idaho law pegs that value to market conditions on January 1. Staff look at what it costs to build and at recent sales, and sometimes they walk the property.

The primary roll notices are mailed by the first Monday of June at the latest. A parcel that was missed lands on the subsequent roll, and those notices come by the fourth Monday in November. Whatever is still unassessed gets picked up by the first Monday in January.

Your notice is also available through the Assessor's online property records. Before you list or sign anything, compare it with what you know about the house. A wrong square footage, a bathroom that was never counted, or a carport recorded as a garage can be corrected by the office, and a clean record makes pricing easier.

How to appeal an Ada County assessment

Appeals go to the Commissioner's Office, which acts as the Board of Equalization and sets your hearing. The form is due there at 5:00 p.m. on the fourth Monday of June.

  • Get the form online, at the Assessor's Office (190 East Front Street, Suite 107) or at the Commissioner's Office (200 W. Front Street, 3rd Floor, Boise).
  • Only market value can be challenged. The amount of tax is off the table.
  • Bring five sets of your paperwork: the original, plus copies for each Commissioner and for the Assessor.
  • Name a contact person on the form, whether that is you or a representative.

Many owners start earlier, with a conversation with the deputy assessor who worked on the parcel. The county suggests bringing a Realtor's comparative market analysis, an independent appraisal or repair estimates. Values do get adjusted at that stage now and then.

Expect a high bar. The county treats the assessor's number as correct unless you prove otherwise with clear and convincing evidence. Closed sales from the market help you; opinions do not. If you will sell in spring, spell out in the sale agreement who handles a June appeal.

Due dates and penalties

Pay the whole year, or the first half, by December 20. The second half is due June 20 of the next year. For 2026 taxes, the first installment is due by December 21, 2026, because the 20th is a Sunday.

DateWhat happens
January 1Value is fixed; first day to apply for the homeowner's exemption or Circuit Breaker
First Monday in JuneAssessment notices go out
June 20Final day for the prior year's second half before a late charge
Fourth Monday in JuneFinal day to file an assessment appeal
Fourth Monday in NovemberPrimary roll bills go out
December 20Full year or first half due

Late payments cost a 2% charge, and interest of 1% a month begins the following January 1. If the 20th lands on a weekend or holiday, a postmark on the 20th still counts the next business day. Notices for unpaid first halves go out in January, and for unpaid second halves in July.

What happens to the tax bill when an Ada County house changes hands?

A change of owner triggers a separate "missed" roll bill in February, covering the period from the transfer date through December 31. Buyers and sellers who expect the regular December bill to settle everything are sometimes surprised.

Improvements and newly occupied construction go onto the subsequent (occupancy) roll. Those bills usually arrive in January with a June due date. A seller who finished an addition or a new build late in the year should plan on one.

Think of the calendar as two cycles layered together. One is the assessment cycle, which runs from the January value date through the June notices and appeals. The other is the billing cycle, which runs from the November bills through the December and June payments. A listing date that sits between them, say in the middle of summer, usually means the buyer inherits a bill you already know the size of.

Before closing, have the title company look up the balance and search for open missed-roll or subsequent-roll bills. For questions, the Treasurer's Office is at 208-287-6800, and its online payment site shows bills and payment history.

Homestead and other exemptions

The homeowner's exemption takes 50% off the taxable value of an owner-occupied primary home and up to one acre of land, capped by the state at $125,000 for 2021 through 2025. It stays with you only while you own and live in the home. Once ownership changes or the house stops being your primary residence, it ends, and the next owner files fresh.

  • Homeowner's exemption: apply through the county Assessor.
  • Property Tax Reduction (Circuit Breaker): income-based, with an Assessor application as well.

If you sell early in the year, let your buyer know the exemption will not carry over. Their first bill will look different from yours.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Ada County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What to gather before you list

A short folder of paperwork saves you phone calls later. Pull the latest assessment notice from the Assessor's online records and check the square footage, bathroom count and garage description. Print the Treasurer's payment history so you can see which halves are paid. If you built or finished anything in the past year, note the date, because that decides whether a subsequent-roll bill is coming.

Then hand the folder to your title company or agent. Ada County's Assessor handles value, the Commissioners handle appeals, and the Treasurer handles bills and payments. Calling the right office first keeps a simple question from turning into a week of transfers. Write down the name of anyone who gives you a figure by phone, and ask for it by email when the amount matters at closing.

Selling with taxes owed

Falling behind gets expensive fast, since 1% interest each month is charged on the tax and the late charge together after January 1. Inherited houses, rentals and homes with deferred repairs are the usual cases, often because nobody was opening the mail.

A sale is still possible. Escrow pays the tax out of your proceeds, and the title company produces an exact payoff. A sensible order of work:

  1. Call the Treasurer's Office for the current balance, including the late charge and interest.
  2. Ask whether any missed-roll or subsequent-roll bill is open.
  3. Give the payoff to the title company so it appears on your closing statement.
  4. Weigh each offer against a listing's net after repairs and holding costs.

A cash sale can move faster than a listing because there is no lender underwriting to wait on. We buy as is, so you do not need to repair anything first. Call or text for a written offer on an Ada County house. If it does not work for you, you owe us nothing.

Frequently asked questions

Where do I pay Ada County property tax?

Pay the Ada County Treasurer online through the county's payment site or by mail. Bills and payment history are online, and the office answers at 208-287-6800.

What is the Ada County property tax appeal deadline?

The form is due at 5:00 p.m. on the fourth Monday of June at the Commissioner's Office. Only the value can be appealed, not the tax amount.

Is the 2026 first installment due on December 20?

No. Because December 20 is a Sunday, it is due by December 21, 2026.

Does the homeowner's exemption move to the buyer?

No. It ends when ownership changes or the home stops being your primary residence, so the new owner has to apply.

Can I sell an Ada County house if I owe back taxes?

Yes. Escrow pays the balance, including the 2% late charge and monthly interest, from your proceeds. Get a payoff figure from the title company before accepting an offer.

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Kootenai County?

Kootenai County in brief

Kootenai County is in the Idaho Panhandle, and Coeur d'Alene serves as both county seat and largest city. The population has roughly tripled since 1980, from 59,770 to an estimated 191,864 in 2025. Newer subdivisions around Post Falls and Rathdrum now sit near older housing close to the lake and downtown.

Fourteen incorporated cities share the county, among them Athol, Coeur d'Alene, Dalton Gardens, Hayden, Post Falls, Rathdrum and Spirit Lake. A seller's address might be inside a city, on the water or on rural land, and the rules that apply change with each. Growth shows up in the tax rolls too, since districts keep adjusting to a bigger base of homes. Many residents also work across the state line, with 5,031 county residents holding jobs in Spokane, Washington.

Snow, roofs and building rules

The county uses its own snow load map and its own amendments to the building code, so a roof is measured against a local standard. The residential permit guide sets a minimum frost depth of 24 inches for footings, and the county adopted its current construction codes by Ordinance 608, effective January 1, 2020.

Manufactured and mobile homes get specific treatment under Title 7 of the county code. A legally set home that meets county and state rules can be relocated without extra proof if it can be verified as built for a roof snow load of at least 30 pounds per square foot. If you are selling one, gather the data plate and any permits before you list.

Missing permits tend to surface at the worst moment, right after an inspection. Ask the county building office what permits are on file for a finished basement, a deck or a shop before a buyer asks. Older homes near the lake tend to draw closer looks at the roof, wiring and foundation.

Billing and due dates

The county mails every tax notice by the fourth Monday of November. Payment is due on or before December 20. Not getting a bill does not excuse the tax, under Idaho Code 63-902(9).

Payment methodHow it works
MailCounts as on time only with a USPS postmark on or before the due date
In personPay at the counter instead of by mail
OnlineCredit card at kcgov.us; the payer covers transaction fees
Phone208-446-1005, option 3

Interest on delinquent tax runs at one percent per month starting January 1. Treat the December 20 date as firm, and note that an appeal does not pause payment.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Kootenai County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

What happens after three years unpaid?

Kootenai County follows a tax deed track. Once real property taxes are three years delinquent, the tax collector sends the recorded owner a Pending Issue of Tax Deed letter. To stop the process, the owner must pay the third year in full. Partial payments are applied to the balance but do not stop it.

An owner who cannot pay can apply to the Board of County Commissioners for hardship relief at 208-446-1600. Parcels that reach the end of the process go to a tax deed auction. If this describes your house, an early sale or payoff through escrow protects whatever equity you have.

How to appeal your assessment

The deadline is the fourth Monday in June. The only way to file is through the Board of County Commissioners' office at 208-446-1600. The Board of Equalization hearing runs like a court and acts in a quasi-judicial role, so prepare accordingly.

Bring evidence that the assessed value is wrong: a recent appraisal, repair estimates or documentation of damage. Keep paying on schedule while the appeal is open.

Two offices split the work, and calling the wrong one costs time. The assessor handles value and appeals. The treasurer handles bills, payments and delinquencies.

Recording a deed

The Recorder charges $10 for the first page and $3 for each additional page of standard documents. Surveys are $5.00 a page, plats are $11.00 and copies of recorded documents are $1.00 a page. State law sets a $15.00 fee for deeds of 30 pages or less. The office is open 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., Monday through Friday, excluding holidays.

If an heir, a divorcing spouse or a co-owner is involved, record the deed before the sale instead of waiting for closing. The title company then has the full chain of ownership in hand.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Kootenai County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Who to call for what

Sorting out which office answers which question saves a lot of back and forth. Here is a short directory built from the numbers above.

  • Tax balance, payment questions and payoff totals: the treasurer, 208-446-1005.
  • Appeals and hardship relief: the Board of County Commissioners' office, 208-446-1600.
  • Permits on file for a deck, shop or finished basement: the county building office.
  • Deed recording and copies of recorded documents: the Recorder, open weekdays from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.

Write down who you spoke with and what number they gave you. If a payoff figure will be used at closing, ask for it in writing so the title company can match it to the settlement statement.

Getting the house ready for a sale

Buyers in North Idaho look hard at anything tied to weather. Have the roof checked against the local snow load standard if the house is older, and know the age of the heating system. If you own a manufactured home, find the data plate early, since it is the document that proves the roof snow load rating.

Property tax is the other half of the file. Print the treasurer's balance, confirm both halves are current and keep the mailing postmark or receipt for any payment you made by mail. A clean tax record tells a buyer the house has no hidden liens waiting at closing, and it lets a cash buyer or an agent quote a firm timeline.

If the house sits on a lake, on rural land or inside a smaller city such as Athol or Spirit Lake, ask the title company whether any additional district or city charges appear on the bill. Rules differ by address, and the surprise is usually in the details of a particular parcel.

Closing day on a Kootenai County sale

Plan the last week backward from the title company's closing date. Confirm the payoff total a few days ahead, not that morning. Gather the deed information, any lake or rural parcel details and the names of everyone on title, because a co-owner who is missing from the paperwork can delay recording.

After closing, the recorder files the deed and the treasurer's records follow. Hold on to your copy of the settlement statement and one confirmation that taxes were paid, so a later question about a bill has a paper trail.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Selling when taxes are owed

You can sell a house with unpaid property tax. Call the treasurer at 208-446-1005 for an exact payoff total, then have the title or escrow company pay it out of your proceeds. The county warns that escrow may not pay the treasurer if closing happens before annual tax information is available, so confirm in writing that the tax is actually paid after closing.

A typical sequence looks like this:

  1. Get the payoff total from the treasurer.
  2. Tell the title company about every unpaid year, not only the current one.
  3. Ask whether the closing falls before or after annual tax information is released.
  4. Keep your settlement statement and a receipt from the treasurer.

When a deed process is looming, speed matters, and a cash purchase removes the wait for a buyer's loan approval. We take houses in whatever shape they are in, and turning an offer down costs you nothing. Set it beside what a listing would put in your pocket before choosing.

Frequently asked questions

What is the county seat of Kootenai County?

Coeur d'Alene is both the county seat and the largest city.

When are Kootenai County property tax bills mailed?

Notices go out by the fourth Monday of November, and the tax is payable on or before December 20.

How do I appeal my Kootenai County property assessment?

Contact the Board of County Commissioners' office at 208-446-1600 by the fourth Monday in June. The hearing before the Board of Equalization works like a court proceeding.

What happens after three years of unpaid property tax in Kootenai County?

The tax collector sends the recorded owner a Pending Issue of Tax Deed letter. Paying the third year in full stops the process, and partial payments do not.

Can I sell a Kootenai County house with unpaid property tax?

Yes. Get the exact payoff from the treasurer at 208-446-1005 and have the title or escrow company pay it from your proceeds. Escrow may not pay the treasurer if closing comes before annual tax information is available.

Canyon County, ID Property Tax Guide: Offices, Appeals and Selling With Tax Due

Selling in Canyon County? Get a Cash Offer

We buy Canyon County houses as-is and reply with a written cash offer.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Canyon County?
We buy Canyon County houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Canyon County for homeowners

Canyon County lies west of Ada County in the Boise metro area. Caldwell is the county seat and Nampa is the biggest city. Nine cities fall inside its lines: Caldwell, Nampa, Middleton, Parma, Greenleaf, Melba, Notus and Wilder, plus Star, which is mostly in Ada County.

The 2025 population is 275,123 and the 2024 median household income is $76,488. Commuting shapes the housing market. In 2023, about 49,391 workers lived and worked in the county, while 65,317 residents drove out for work, most often to Boise. A job change in the Treasure Valley can put a Canyon County household on a moving deadline.

Who handles property tax?

Two elected offices share the job. The Assessor sets the value, and the Treasurer sends bills, takes payments and passes the money to the taxing districts. The Commissioners double as the Board of Equalization and must finish and adjourn by the second Monday in July.

  • Assessor: 111 N. 11th Ave, Suite 250, Caldwell; 208-454-7431; 2cAsr@canyoncounty.id.gov.
  • Treasurer: 111 N. 11th Ave, Suite 240, Caldwell; 208-454-7354; treas@canyoncounty.id.gov.

Under Idaho Code 63-205, assessed value has to match market value as of January 1. Every property gets a fresh appraisal on a five-year cycle, and values are trended in the years between. The county stresses that taxes follow budgets, not assessments. Local budgets can grow only 3% plus new construction value, yet your own bill can still climb while your home's value stays flat, because the dollars the districts need get spread over the whole tax base.

How a Canyon County bill is calculated

The formula is simple: taxable value multiplied by the combined levy rate of every district that serves your parcel. Four layers make up the rate: county, school, city and special districts. The state certifies the levy rates by the end of October, and the Treasurer posts the current list.

Your own numbers are on your notice, and the Assessor's assessment information page explains each line. Look at the homeowner's exemption line first, because it halves the taxable value of an owner-occupied home and up to an acre of land, up to $125,000 for 2021 through 2025. If that line is blank on a house you live in, call the Assessor.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Canyon County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How to appeal an assessment

You start with an informal review. If that fails, the appeal goes to the Board of Equalization by the fourth Monday in June. Only the assessment can be appealed, never the tax itself.

  • First ground: the record is wrong, for instance one bath listed instead of two, a carport recorded as a garage or 1,600 square feet recorded as 2,000.
  • Second ground: the market value is too high, shown by similar properties that sold for less before January 1 of the current year.
  • Informal review: a meeting, call or email with the deputy assessor for your area. A corrected notice usually follows within two to three weeks.
  • Formal appeal: a written form, obtained from the person who did the review and filed under Idaho Code 63-501A.

Only arm's-length sales that closed before January 1 count, and later sales are not admissible. If you lose, the next stops are the Idaho Board of Tax Appeals and then district court under Idaho Code 63-511. A hardship exemption application for the current year is also due June 20 and goes to the Board of Equalization.

Due dates and penalties

Notices go out by the fourth Monday in November.

PaymentDue dateIf late
First halfDecember 202% late charge; interest of 1% per month from January 1 on the tax and the charge, which the county also describes as 12% a year
Second halfJune 20 of the next yearPenalty and interest apply
New construction supplementJune 20, notice mailed in March or AprilProrated from occupancy or completion to December 31 of the prior year
Returned checkAny time$20 fee

Personal property and manufactured housing become fully delinquent if the first half is unpaid on December 20, and the whole tax comes due.

The county reports no formal monthly payment plan, so the two halves are your only schedule. A missing notice is no excuse for a missed payment, citing Idaho Code 63-902(9). If you bought during the year and never got a bill, call the Treasurer's office.

Programs that lower a bill

Three programs run through the Assessor. The homeowner's exemption is covered above. The other programs have windows of their own:

  • Property Tax Reduction (Circuit Breaker): income based, with applications from January 1 through April 15.
  • Disabled-owner benefit: up to $1,500 off the bill for homeowners who are 100% service-connected disabled, on a primary residence and up to an acre, same January 1 to April 15 window.
  • Homeowner Tax Relief credit: goes to properties with a homeowner's exemption in effect before the second Monday in July.

Relief programs shift from year to year. An Additional Tax Relief credit that existed in 2023 was not offered for 2024. Check the Treasurer's page for the current year before you promise a buyer any figure.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Canyon County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What to have ready before you list

Start at the Assessor's office, which keeps the property record. Ask for a printout and walk the house with it. Bath counts, square footage and the garage or carport description are the entries most worth checking, since the same errors people appeal are the ones that confuse buyers.

Next, call the Treasurer and ask which halves are paid, whether any supplemental notice is open and what the balance looks like today. Write down the date you called. If the house is new construction or recently finished, the supplemental bill is the item most likely to surface after you have already agreed on a closing date.

Last, tell your title company about any homeowner's exemption, hardship application or Circuit Breaker filing tied to the property. Those programs depend on who owns and lives in the house, and a sale changes the answer for the buyer.

Selling with taxes owed

Three situations come up again and again: a missed December payment, an inherited house nobody is paying on, and a supplemental new-construction bill that arrives after a sale is already planned. At 12% a year, a late first half grows quickly.

Unpaid tax is settled through escrow at closing, and the title company can quote the exact payoff. Ask the Treasurer for balances on every parcel in the sale, and confirm whether a supplemental notice is still coming.

We buy houses as is in Canyon County, so a seller with a delinquent balance does not have to repair or clean before an offer. Call or text for a written cash offer. If you decline, you owe us nothing.

Frequently asked questions

When is the Canyon County appeal deadline?

The deadline for the regular roll is the fourth Monday in June, under Idaho Code 63-501A. Begin with an informal review before that date.

What is the Canyon County late fee for property tax?

A 2% late charge is added to an unpaid first half, and interest runs at 1% per month from January 1, which the county also describes as 12% a year.

Can I pay Canyon County property tax in installments?

Yes, in two halves: December 20 and June 20. There is no formal monthly payment plan.

Can I appeal because my taxes are too high?

No. Idaho allows appeals of the assessed value only. Budget complaints go to the elected officials who set the budgets.

Do I need to pay Canyon County taxes if I never got a notice?

Yes. Under Idaho Code 63-902(9), not receiving a notice does not excuse the tax, late charge or interest.
